desc:
A broken calculator shows the number start. It has only two buttons: double (multiply the displayed number by 2) and decrement (subtract 1). Each press is one step.

Return the minimum number of steps needed to make the display show exactly target.

start = 2, target = 3  -> 2   (2 -> 4 -> 3)
start = 5, target = 8  -> 2   (5 -> 4 -> 8)
start = 3, target = 10 -> 3   (3 -> 6 -> 5 -> 10)
start = 9, target = 4  -> 5   (only decrements)
hints: Forward search blows up: from start you can go both up and down. What if you work from target back to start?
Reversed, the operations become: halve (if the value is even) or add 1. When target is at most start, only decrements are useful.
While target is larger than start: if it is odd, add 1 (halving is impossible), otherwise halve it. Count each move. When target drops to start or below, add the remaining difference start - target.
editorial: Run the process backwards from target: the inverse of doubling is halving (only legal for even numbers) and the inverse of decrementing is adding 1. As long as target > start we want to shrink the value as fast as possible. If it is even, halving is clearly the best move. If it is odd we are forced to add 1 first; adding 1 and halving costs two steps, and any alternative that adds more before halving reaches a number at least as large with at least as many steps.

Once target ≤ start doubling can no longer help (it only moves away), so the rest are plain decrements: start - target more steps. Each loop turn at least halves the target, giving O(log target) time.
